title: The Belly and the Members
text:
Once the parts of the body held a meeting and made a complaint. The hands worked from morning to night, the feet walked everywhere, the mouth chewed and the teeth ground, and all of it went to the belly, which lay at the center doing nothing but receiving. Why, they asked, should they slave for a lazy master?

So they went on strike. The hands stopped carrying food, the mouth refused to open, and the teeth would not chew. For a day or two the members felt pleased with themselves. Then the hands grew weak, the legs began to shake, and the eyes went dim. The whole body was wasting away, and the members discovered too late that the belly, quiet as it seemed, had been turning their food into the strength that kept every one of them alive.

The Roman historian Livy tells how this fable was put to use. In 494 BC the common people of Rome, angry at the patricians, walked out of the city and camped on a hill. The senate sent Menenius Agrippa, a man the people trusted, and he told them only this story. According to Livy, the comparison worked: the people saw that the city and its classes depended on one another, and talks began that brought them back.
lesson: Before you decide that a quieter part of your team contributes nothing, find out what it actually does. Pulling out of a shared effort usually hurts you too.
people: The belly and the members; Menenius Agrippa
date: c. 6th century BC; told in Rome in 494 BC according to Livy
source: Aesop's Fables, The Belly and the Members; Livy, History of Rome (Ab Urbe Condita) 2.32
caveat: Livy wrote about four centuries after the secession, and the scene with Menenius may be a later embellishment.
